title: Video Streaming (Netflix / YouTube)
summary: Design an on-demand video platform: upload or ingest, transcode, and stream smoothly to billions of viewers worldwide.
statement: Design a video streaming service. Creators or studios upload videos; viewers watch them on many devices and networks with minimal buffering. Include processing, storage, delivery, and a basic recommendation entry point. Start by clarifying requirements and estimating scale, then design the system and defend your decisions.
initialGuidance: Clarify the users, the main journeys, and what is explicitly out of scope before drawing anything.
Estimate read and write volume and storage growth; the numbers decide which components you need.
Name the guarantees you will offer (consistency, durability, availability) and the trade-offs behind them.
Write down assumptions as you make them and revisit them when requirements change.
coreFunctionalRequirements: Transcode into multiple resolutions and formats.

requirementQuestions.question: How many videos, uploads per day, concurrent viewers, and hours watched?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Sets read and write rates and storage growth, which decide whether a single node can cope.

requirementQuestions.question: What start-up time and rebuffering rate is acceptable?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Defines which paths need caching, precomputation, or regional placement.

requirementQuestions.question: User-generated content or a curated catalogue?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Fixes what is in and out of the design so effort goes to what matters.

requirementQuestions.question: What is the budget for bandwidth and storage, and who pays for CDN egress?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Prevents over-engineering and affects build-versus-buy choices.

requirementQuestions.question: Is DRM or content protection needed?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Introduces authentication, authorisation, and privacy constraints that affect the design.

requirementQuestions.question: How should playback behave during regional failures?
requirementQuestions.whyItMatters: Determines redundancy and failover design, and which features may degrade instead of failing.

workloadAssumptions.illustrativeNote: All numbers below are illustrative examples for practice and are not benchmarks. Real answers depend on the requirements the candidate negotiates.

estimationPrompts: What peak egress bandwidth does 20 million viewers generate?
How much storage do renditions of a day of uploads need?
How much transcoding compute is required per hour of upload?

keyDecisions.question: How do videos enter the system?
considerations: Chunked resumable uploads to object storage.

keyDecisions.question: How are renditions produced?
considerations: Split the video into segments and transcode in parallel (DAG of tasks).

keyDecisions.question: How is playback adapted to networks?
considerations: Segment-based protocols (HLS, DASH) with multiple bitrates.
Client chooses the rendition from a manifest.
Short segments reduce latency but increase requests.

keyDecisions.question: How is content delivered globally?
considerations: CDN with edge caches; popular titles pushed to edges.
Cache hierarchy and tail content on origin.

keyDecisions.question: Where do catalogue and playback state live?
considerations: Watch-progress writes are frequent; use a scalable store.

tradeoffs.tension: Better quality coverage versus storage and compute.
Hit rate versus bandwidth spent on unwatched content.

commonMistakes: Transcoding a whole file on one machine.
A single resolution with no adaptive bitrate.
Ignoring that popular content dominates and the long tail does not cache.
followUps: How do you minimise start-up time?
How do you handle a hit release causing a traffic surge?
How would you add live streaming?
